lede: From the approval of the rule to the deaths in exile. Dates in the texts are given as printed; for what the texts carried here do not date, the timeline follows modern accounts and says so.

stations.text: Innocent III approves by word of mouth the way of life of Francis of Assisi and his first brothers: to follow the Gospel without property. (Modern accounts.)
Honorius III confirms the definitive rule: the brothers shall appropriate nothing to themselves, neither house nor place nor anything else. John XXII quotes the words a century later.

Gregory IX (Quo elongati, 1230) interprets the rule: the brothers have the use of things, not their ownership. Innocent IV (Ordinem vestrum, 1245) declares the ownership to belong to the Roman Church. (Modern accounts.)

Nicholas III defines Franciscan poverty: renunciation of ownership individually and in common is the way of Christ; the friars have only the simple use of fact; glossing the decretal is forbidden on pain of excommunication.

At the Council of Vienne, Clement V hears the Spirituals' complaints against the Community and rules between them: granaries only in real need, 'poor use' as far as the rule states it, and neither side may call the other heretical.

After a two-year vacancy the cardinals at Lyon elect Jacques Duèze, a canon lawyer from Cahors, then in his seventies. In the same year the Franciscans elect Michael of Cesena their minister general. (Modern accounts.)
Sixty-four Spirituals from Narbonne and Béziers wait all night before the papal palace at Avignon. Their spokesmen are arrested one by one; twenty-five of them are handed to the inquisitor.
The pope orders the Spirituals to put off their short habits and obey their superiors: 'obedience is the greatest good'.
Four Spiritual Franciscans who refused to obey are burned as heretics. The Beguins of Languedoc venerate them as martyrs, and over the next years the inquisitors burn Beguins who say so.

Dante, in the last years of his life at Ravenna, has Thomas Aquinas tell the life of Francis as a marriage to Poverty, widowed since Christ. He dies in September 1321, half a year before the pope opens the question of Christ's poverty.

An inquisitor declares heretical a Beguin's assertion that Christ and the apostles had nothing, individually or in common; a Franciscan lector objects that this contradicts Exiit. The question goes to the pope. (Modern accounts.)
John XXII suspends the ban on disputing Exiit: 'hidden truth is often opened by arguments'.

The Franciscan general chapter, under Michael of Cesena, declares that to say Christ and the apostles had nothing by right of property 'individually and in common' is 'not heretical, but sound, catholic and faithful'. Forty-one masters of the order at Paris and in England approve.

stations.titel: Four Beguins to the secular arm
stations.text: At a general sermon in Saint-Étienne of Toulouse, Bernard Gui hands Guillaume Ruffi, Pierre Dominici, Pierre Hospitalis and Pierre Guiraud to the king's judge, 'short of death and the mutilation of limbs'. Dominici had kept a litany with the names of about seventy condemned Beguins; Hospitalis held that the pope who allowed the friars granaries had ceased to be pope.
The Roman Church renounces its ownership of the friars' goods: the Franciscans are made owners against their will.
The order's procurator Bonagratia of Bergamo appeals in consistory against Ad conditorem and is thrown into 'a dark prison' for a year less twenty days.
John XXII canonizes the Dominican theologian at Avignon, four months before condemning the Franciscan doctrine. (Modern accounts.)
The assertion that Christ and the apostles had nothing, 'nor even in common', is declared heretical.

Bernard Gui finishes his Practica, with a chapter on the Beguins: their houses of poverty, their martyrs of Marseille, the bones of the burned kept as relics, and the questions to ask them. In 1324 he leaves the inquisition to become bishop of Lodève.

Louis the Bavarian, excommunicated by the pope in March, appeals against 'John, who calls himself pope' to a general council, in the chapel of the Teutonic Order at Sachsenhausen by Frankfurt. A chapter on the poverty of Christ, drafted by Franciscans at his court, declares the pope a heretic by his own decretals.
The pope rejects the 'key of knowledge' and declares the defenders of the condemned doctrine heretics.
Marsilius of Padua completes his treatise against the temporal power of the clergy, with a long section on evangelical poverty; he flees to Louis in 1326. (Modern accounts.)

Four months after receiving Michael 'peacefully and kindly', John XXII calls him a supporter of heretics before a cardinal and three friars, declares the Perugia letter heretical, and forbids him to leave the curia. Four days later Michael appeals in secret.

On 13 April 1328 Michael of Cesena appeals secretly against the pope in the Franciscan convent of Avignon; on the night of 26 May he flees with William of Ockham and Bonagratia to a galley sent by the emperor. On 12 December he fixes his appeal to the doors of the cathedral of Pisa.

Michael is deposed at Bologna (1328); at Paris on Pentecost 1329 the order elects Gerald Odonis and declares that the pope 'had defined well on the poverty of Christ'. John XXII answers Michael in the bull Quia vir reprobus (16 November 1329).
At Munich, under the emperor's protection, Ockham answers the pope's bull Quia vir reprobus phrase by phrase, and defines a right as a power one can defend in court.

John XXII preaches that the souls of the blessed will not see God face to face until the Last Judgement; the Franciscan exiles in Munich call him a heretic again. He retracts on his deathbed and dies on 4 December 1334. (Modern accounts.)
Michael of Cesena dies in Munich on 29 November 1342, William of Ockham there in 1347. (Modern accounts.)

Umberto Eco sets Il nome della rosa in November 1327, at an abbey where a papal delegation and Michael of Cesena's friars meet to debate the poverty of Christ. The meeting is fiction; the dispute is the one documented here.
